To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Hebbian weight changes driven by a global feedback signal can optimize the performance of an artificial network, (2) the same learning rule can reproduce experimentally observed network dynamics in a brain-computing interface learning task, (3) the model can learn within biologically realistic time frames, and (4) the learning rule does not require extraneous information to separate noise and signal.
a Hebbian learning rule with a reward-modulated weight update can reproduce the observed network reorganization during brain-computer interface training.

(1) a reward-driven learning rule that does not require extracellular information can reproduce the observed changes in the tuning properties of motor cortex neurons, and (2) a model of this kind, with biologically realistic parameters, is able to optimize a motor cortical decoding system within biologically relevant periods of time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the observed learning effects can be explained by the reward-driven Hebbian learning rule proposed here.
the development and testing of biologically plausible learning rules.
the question of whether the brain can learn to control external devices by using a simple reward-modulated Hebbian rule.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a Hebbian learning rule that is driven by a global error signal and noise can reproduce the learning effects observed in the brain-computer experiment.
the reward-driven Hebbian learning rule proposed here is able to reproduce the experimentally observed learning effects.

the reward-driven Hebbian learning rule is able, under biologically realistic conditions, to produce the experimentally observed network changes in a brain control system, thus providing a possible explanation for these effects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a learning rule that can explain experimentally measured reorganization of neuronal tuning properties in a brain control paradigm.
we have proposed an explanation for the experimentally observed reorganization of the motor cortical network that is based on a simple, local, unsupervised learning rule.
we show a reward-modulated Hebbian learning rule that is able to explain experimentally observed reorganization in a motor cortical network.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the observed changes in the neuronal tuning curves can be understood in the context of reward-modulated Hebbian learning.
the observed changes in tuning can be explained as the consequence of an unsupervised Hebbian learning rule that uses only the reward signal and neuronal spike trains as input.

the reward-modulated Hebbian learning rule provides a simple and plausible mechanism to explain how the brain learns to adapt its control signals to compensate for errors in a task that requires the brain to control a computer interface.
